Aaron: The boy who can't eat

By: Diana Lucas | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Summary:
Three, year old Aaron Lipschitz has a rare incurable disease that affects his immune system. It’s called Interleukin-12 Receptor Defect and of the known cases world wide he is the only one who is unable to consume food.
Now with over R 1.24 million raised from crowd funding platform BackaBuddy, the boy who can’t eat might be able to have a chance at a normal life.


Further information:
When Aaron was two weeks old his parents Taryn and Steven noticed Aaron was responding negatively to his feeds and rushed him to hospital. That was the first of many hospital visits and countless tests which eventually found Aaron was not only among the 0.1% of babies who are born allergic to breast milk protein but that any food item, formula or liquid – excluding water causes severe pain and discomfort to Aaron.
“It's still so difficult to process. We are an average couple without any significant medical history so to have such a unique child as been really surprising to us” For Taryn, a play therapist, this was a complete surprise she had an easy pregnancy and uncomplicated birth.
For the first two years of his life, Aaron had to take a pancreatic enzyme pill called Creon in order to digest an expensive formula called Neocate, which he had to take every 2 to 3 hours. His body couldn’t tolerate anything else. Then in October last year the doctors could see the formula was no longer providing Aaron with enough nutrition to accommodate his growth and he had to be in effect treated like a coma patient, he was fitted with central lines and catheters, a port runs through Aarons heart and every evening he is fed intravenously, avoiding his digestive system.
Now at 3 years old, Aaron is no stranger to the hospital. He’s been exposed to blood tests, drips, ultrasounds, hundreds of hospital visits, MRIs, consultations with immunologists, gastroenterologists, neurologists, paediatricians, allergists, haematologists, oncologists, dieticians and occupational therapists to name a few. His party trick, he can recite all his medications no mean feat considering how many he has.
Most afternoons Aaron can be found at the Cape Town Mediclinic under the care and observation of Dr Deon Smith. To help his immune system to work more effectively, needles are inserted into his legs to administer immunoglobulin, without this Aaron is vulnerable to infections, at 1 years old Aaron nearly died from septicemia.
Besides being in and out of hospital, Aaron sill attends school, birthday parties and goes grocery shopping with his mom. At this stage, he seems undeterred by food as it’s something he is unfamiliar with.
 
 “Aaron understands that he can't eat because food makes him sick. He doesn't show much interest in food because he hasn't experienced eating so doesn't really know what he is missing out on. We don't feel comfortable eating in front of him because we can't share our food with him. We think he might be starting to notice that there might be something different about him, but thankfully he is still young enough that he is not self-conscious about his feeding port or NG tube. “

The only hope of Aaron leading a healthy life will require multiple chemotherapy sessions and eventually a bone marrow transplant when a donor match is found. Specialists would essentially need to build Aaron a new immune system.
This is an expensive process and in January last year Taryn and Steven launched a campaign on the donations based crowd funding platform BackaBuddy. Their target R 1 500 000 and in just one year they have secured R 1 245 350. 57 +. The donations have ranged from R 100 to R 300 and have come from not just South Africa but all around the world.
“We have been completely blown away by our BackaBuddy experience. For the first 3 years of Aaron's life we tried to manage without community support, both emotional and financially. It was a big step for us to share Aaron's story and ask for the help we need. Our BackaBuddy campaign has completely exceeded our expectations.”
It’s not difficult to see why the public has fallen in love with Aaron. He’s a charismatic boy who has a zest for life an adventure, but Aaron’s road to recovery will be a long one.

Press Release:


The Boy Who Can’t Eat
Three-year-old Aaron Lipschitz has become known as the boy who can’t eat. He’s the first South African diagnosed with Interleukin-12 Receptor Defect, a rare disease that affects his immune system. He’s fed through an intravenous feeding port every night to keep him alive. Despite the odds, Aaron is fighting on and may be just weeks away from a life-changing bone marrow transplant. Carte Blanche meets this remarkable young survivor.


Script:


Link
Three year old, Aaron Lipschitz has never eaten he survives on expensive formulas fed through tubes but there is hope that all is about to change.

V/O 10 sec
Its been a long road for Aaron and his parents Steven and Taryn …..even diagnosing his condition , has been an ongoing challenge for medical specialists.

Link: Taryn had a normal pregnancy and no alarm bells rang with the doctors when Aaron was born but after a few weeks at home there were the first signs of what was to become a very long journey.

Taryn Lipschitz
Taryn: I remember us to driving to Mediclinic and we had wet towels all over him in the car and Ya that was his first admission at 2 weeks since then we have kind of been in and out.

V/O 5 sec
Aaron’s doctor, Deon Smith was there at his first ER admission.

Dr Deon Smith
Paediatrician
Dr Deon Smith: We were a bit surprised a breast fed baby getting d but can happen 2/ 3 days home…she kept phoning not doing well he’s doing a lot of crying, he’s vomiting then it became increasing apparent that he’s not doing well had him been admitted again because of the severity of his symptoms

V/O 17 and a half
Aaron was a rare case, a baby allergic to breast milk and that was only the start. …. any food or even a trace of food set off violent reactions. He has only been able to have a hyperallergenic formula, Neocate..and water for the last three years.

Taryn: He’s never had a meal, we had some unsuccessful food trials we’ve boiled a carrot or potato in water and given a syringe of the water and then he’s been sick for weeks for that.

V/O 12 sec
Aaron’s intimate relationship with all things medical became the new norm. Specialists from dietician’s to gastroenterologist’s became part of the team to diagnose what exactly was wrong with Aaron.

Dion: This is the three volumes that make up AL in my practice those are notes copies of blood results… copies of correspondence at one point the file s weighed more than he did.
Derek: Three files at age of three is something else?
Dion It gives you an idea of severity of the problem and belies his appearance, as challenging as it has been working Aaron makes it all worth while and you cant help but go that extra mile.
Steven Lipschitz

Steven: It felt like we were on an episode of House …you know how they check boxes it’s not this it’s not this…

Aaron: “ Twinkle Twinkle…..how I wonder where you are”

V/O 13 sec
Neocate which is a formula for babies was not nutritious enough, so in October last year, he went on to Total Parenatal Nutrition where Aaron is fed from an intravenous feeding port straight into the right ventricle of his heart.

Up Sound Taryn: “ And then we open this up at night….. two super powers”

Dr Deon: His parents were trained to do that under strict aseptic technique because you cannot allow infection into that whole process.
Derek: What has it cost you additionally with Aaron’s condition?
Steven: we have wiped our savings we’ve…
Taryn: To put it into perspective a tin of Neocate is about R 480 and the first two years our medical aid did not cover that and at some stages he was going through a tin of that a day. We always laugh we could have had a house made of Neocate.

Derek: Does he ask for food does he reach out for a chocolate?
Taryn: No when he goes to play school he wants sit at the table wants to he’s got his little bowl of crushed ice and he’s got his water and he wants to be included he wants to sit down and have coffee which for him is crushed ice .

Taryn: He knows he is different we have created a story around his TPN so he calls it his super so he will say tonight will you put spaghetti or chocolate in my TPN

V/O 17 sec
At 1 years old Aaron developed salmonella septicaemia, type C , a recurring infection which increased his emergency admissions. So now twice a week he’s back at the hospital, getting an antibiotic injected into his veins, to prop up his virtually non existent immune system.

Derek: This is really his 2nd home your rooms the hospital?
Dr Dion Smith: Absolutely and what is intriguing about him is he takes an interest in what other people are eating the vending machine here at the hospital is one of his prime visiting places he buys food for other people we are always being dished out packets of food or chocolates.

Steven: Even though it’s expensive thing because he doesn’t eat it makes him happy to feed other people that why I don’t mind doing that.

Prof Esser: I got to know about A before I met him I was getting a background of a child that had a lot of infections and no diagnosis.

Prof Monika Esser
Head of Immunology Unit Tygerberg,

V/O 13 sec
Prof Monika Esser, who heads up the Immunology Unit of Tygerberg Hospital, together with the genetic department at Stellenbosch University, began to investigate how a genetic defect might be the missing link.

Derek: What followed I guess was a lot of very sophisticated detective work?
Prof Esser: Yes he is actually quiet a healthy looking kid from the outside so what are the unusual manifestations that is the detective story the history and it gives you probably the most important clues.

V/O 21 sec
And in October last year they had a breakthrough… after extensive exome( or genetic) sequencing Aaron was diagnosed with Interleukin-12 Receptor defect, an extremely rare incurable disorder, resulting in his inability to fight immune infections… He is the only person South Africa known to have this.

Prof Esser: Coming from both parents they have * an int genetic line being Ash Jews so there is some crowding of genes that could be pathogenic or could cause disease.

Taryn: Yes it’s a recessive condition we each carry half of gene but its such a rare gene the chances of 2 people meeting and having a baby they say its rare in the list of rare
Derek when you did get the eventual diagnosis was it a relief?
Steven: Yes and No It was a relief that all these years we knew something wrong just didn’t know how rare conditions was.

LINK
Taryn and S have high hopes for A’s future but a lot depends on a bone marrow transplant with significant costs but more important possible complications.

Prof Esser: Bone marrow transplant is a bit of a misnomer because we are taking stem cells taking very primitive cells that can transform into new lines of cells …we used to take it from bone marrow and that is where horror comes in but now can be gained from peripheral vein almost like taking blood.
Derek: If Aaron doesn’t have the operation?
Prof Esser I’m not quiet sure what to say to that because his quality of life is severely impaired even though he might look quiet normal when you meet him …hes a lovely little boy he is running out of time if no treatment.

V/O 7 and a half sec
What is still an unknown factor is Aaron’s allergy to food and if the transplant will help this condition….

V/O 12 sec
Steven and Taryn have gone public to to try and find a matching donor for Aaron.
They are urgently asking people to register with Sunflower Foundation or the South African Bone Marrow Registry.

Taryn: As soon as we’ve found that Magic Match then the process starts and the initial 2 week chemotherapy eradicate current immune bring in donor blood . when this happens no immune system.

V/O 16 sec
For Steven and Taryn it’s a totally different life from they ever envisaged…they both work, they have to. Taryn half day as play therapist and without the help of her mother and Faith Chikaka, the nurse aid they simply wouldn’t manage.

Taryn and Steven
Steven: We have to do it Day by day, to look into the future you get 10 steps forward and 20 steps.
Taryn: He’s got a lot of love in his life …..everyone makes him feel secure and loved
